items.title: Clunkster
items.text:
GameMaker 8.2 optimization tools and project processing pipeline.

Non-destructive tools:

  • Linter: tree.yyd validator (see ex1.2)
  • Linter: unused assets detector (see ex2.3 and ex3.2)
  • (TODO) Linter: heavy assets detector (RAM & disk size)
  • Cluster boundaries: assets referenced across clusters, directly (see ex2.4) or through the dependency graph (see ex3.3), are moved to Common, with a report and a RAM budget (see ex3.4)
  • Game Juicer (Prod Build): convert assets into external versions and generate code for their loading (see ex4.1; Dehydration)

Lightly destructive tools:

  • (TODO) Backgrounds minifier: strip tilesets of all unused space
  • (TODO) Audio optimizer: optimize audio files via FFmpeg (see ex4.1 (part of Juicer))

Super destructive tools:

  • (TODO) Project crippler (Dev Build): replace assets with lightweight stubs for faster development

Most of the tools depend heavily on asset clustering (i.e. assigning each asset to an isolated group like "StageA", "StageB", "Common" etc.), but some use it only to group console output.

items.title: Usage
items.text:
The tool runs on Python 3.14+.

Given the architectural differences across GameMaker projects, Clunkster is organized as a set of examples that you can copy, and build your own pipeline out of them. The library itself provides functions that handle quirks and facilitate pipeline logic.

Therefore, recommended way of using this project is cloning it, setting up environment (preferably via uv, standard pip also supported) and writing the pipeline by following the examples. Alternatively, run the existing main.py pipeline.

However, before that, I recommend giving following sections a read - they go more in-depth on which projects need these tools, and how to properly apply them.

items.title: Rationale
items.text:
GameMaker 8.2 runner is 32-bit, meaning there's a hard cap on RAM of around 4 GB. Furthermore, certain parts of the engine start having hardware-specific issues at even 2.5 GB of RAM usage.

Also, such large projects take 10-15 seconds to build.

The most effective solution is to split the large project into logical clusters. You have "Common" assets (Player, Block, ...), and stage-specific assets (bStageATiles, StageAPostProc, ...). So, when game is in a room from Stage A, it technically doesn't require assets from Stage B. Unneeded assets can be replaced with lightweight stubs right in the game project.

For dev builds, the tool can nuke all assets except for ones from specified clusters. Optionally, the resulting stubs can be made more noticeable:

  • sprites and backgrounds become pink-black checkerboards
  • sounds get replaced with buzz.wav and/or fiddlesticks.mp3

Prod builds are similar, but we add dynamic loading. The project is copied, only Common cluster is kept in the base executable. The stage-specific assets are packaged into external files ("wet" versions). When the player enters a new stage, the game dynamically loads ("hydrates") the required assets from the disk. Optionally the stubs can be made less noticeable (though you probably should still make them loud):

  • sprites and backgrounds become 2x2 transparent
  • sounds get replaced with null.wav

This is explained more in-depth in Dehydration and subsequent chapters.

To prevent developers from accidentally referencing a StageB sprite inside a StageA object, a dependency linter is included. It builds dependency graph based on static .gml and .txt metafile analysis.

From those dependencies, the tool can:

  • find orphaned assets that are not referenced by anything
  • find assets that reference disallowed clusters
  • construct sets of assets referenced (both directly and indirectly) in each room, and find what a room references without explicitly being marked to load it.

Offending assets are moved to Common (kept loaded at all times), so the game never runs into a stub, and the tool reports every move along with its estimated RAM cost. A RAM budget on those moves stops the build when a bad reference drags too much into Common.

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text:
1. Use this tool only if it's necessary.

    • Setting this up requires a fair bit of technical knowledge (about both GameMaker 8.2 and Python) and can be a headache.
    • I would only recommend using this tool if your game eats more than 1.5 GB of RAM and your project takes more than 10 seconds to build.

  2. Use Git - destructive tools will nuke your project. Some do that by design, others can lead to data loss if misconfigured.

  3. Follow good practices:

    • Keep asset names clean (press broom icon on IDE's top toolbar to run initial checks).
    • Keep assets belonging to certain stage in that stage's folder.
    • Do not reference things from stageA in stageB objects (unless such an object is only placed in a room that guarantees both stages loaded).
    • Reference Common objects in Stage-specific, not the other way around.
      • If this is unavoidable (for example, when making a stage-specific movement gimmick), use "guard scripts" (if room_is_stageA() { ... }).
    • If an asset is shared between multiple stages, then it belongs in Common cluster.
    • DON'T use timelines.
    • DON'T use the dastardly "Treat uninitialized variables as 0 (BAD!!!)" option.
    • Minimize the number of persistent objects (they'll get tagged as referenced in every room).
    • No dynamic asset referencing (tool won't acknowledge those references when building dependency graph):
      • DON'T do math on asset IDs: draw_sprite(sprSpikeUp+2, x, y).
      • DON'T use string execution: execute_string("instance_create(0, 0, obj_enemy_" + string(current_level) + ")").
      • DON'T pass assets via global variables across cluster boundaries: global.current_boss = obj_StageB_Boss (If Stage A reads this global, the analyzer cannot trace such dependency).
      • ^ That rule includes assigning assets to constants.
    • Use only room_goto for room transitions.
    • Use the linter ignore pragma //!clunkster: ignore only in pure data registry scripts (like sound_balance), which only reference assets but don't instantiate them

Other than that, use the modern project format (.gm82) and Python 3.14+ (uv recommended).

Following sections elaborate on the prerequisites, reasons behind them, antipatterns, and how to properly fix them.

items.title: Project & Asset organization
items.text:
Since Clunkster largely relies on splitting assets into clusters, the tool needs a way to automatically generate clusters for each asset. The easiest way is to parse tree.yyd files and takes the name of the root directory as a cluster name, merging those based on a provided config (see [ex1.3]). Therefore, some amount of project keeping is required.

❌ Bad:

Sprites: 

+Enemies
    |sprite83
    |enemy
    |enemy_burn
    |spr_stageA_specific_enemy_that_is_not_encountered_anywhere_else
+StageA
    |a_sprite_that_is_used_to_be_stageA_specific_but_is_in_fact_used_everywhere
+StageFinalBoss_2_Fix_Final
    |enemy
Backgrounds: 
+Stage3
    |bgStage1
    |tileset_that_is_used_everywhere_but_its_in_this_folder_for_reason
    |bgDarkness_2000x200_semitransparent_black_with_spotlight_in_center

While the tool doesn't require you to name things properly, no duplicates can exist in the project. Secondly, since trees now has structural value to our clusterization, you should dedicate some effort to reorganizing things.

✅ Good:

Sprites: 

+sprEnemies
    |sprEnemySpawner
    |sprEnemy
    |sprEnemyBurn
    |sprEnemyPoisoned
+sprStageA
    |sprFireball
+sprStageFinal
    |sprEnemyBuffed
Backgrounds: 
+bgStageA
    |bStageA
+bgStageC
    |bStageC
tCommon

With this well organized asset tree you can write the ALIAS config so they get correctly assigned to their clusters:

ALIAS: dict[str, list[str]] = {
    'StageA': [
        'sprStageA',
        'bgStageA'
    ],
    'StageC': [
        'bgStageC'
    ],
    'Common': [
        'sprEnemies',
        # tCommon was automatically assigned Common cluster,
        # since it's in the root of the tree
    ],
    # ...
}

Even though appropriate naming of the assets isn't required, I recommend cleaning them up now. It would also be a good idea to do manual optimization passes before starting integrating clustering-dependent tools, like Game Juicer (unless you have an "unrunable game" situation like I had when I started making this tool).

items.title: Eradicating dynamic asset referencing
items.text:
I have seen these quite often.

❌ Bad: Doing maths on asset IDs.

// BAD: Analyzer only sees 'spr_player_base', misses the rest
draw_sprite(spr_player_base + current_animation, image_index, x, y)

This logic relies on Game Maker's internal resource order. While the order was made much more predictable in Game Maker 8.2's modern save format, it is still a bit hidden and should not be used in general.

❌ Bad: String execution.

// BAD: Analyzer cannot trace the boss asset
execute_string(str_cat("instance_create(x, y, obj_boss_", current_level,")"))

execute_string requires Game Maker to parse it and build an AST at runtime, which is slow. Any dynamic code execution should generally be limited to functions like variable_*, and those should never reference assets.

Let's take a look at how to fix such things:

✅ Good: Use explicit references directly

// GOOD: All assets are explicitly declared and mapped
switch current_level {
    case "forest": instance_create(x, y, obj_boss_forest) break
    case "volcano": instance_create(x, y, obj_boss_volcano) break
}

✅ Good: 

var _amb;
_amb[0] = "sfx_ambience0"
_amb[1] = "sfx_ambience1"
_amb[2] = "sfx_ambience2"
_amb[3] = "sfx_ambience3"
_amb[4] = "sfx_ambience4"

sound_loop(_amb[irandom(4)])

items.title: Building dependency flow
items.text:
A healthy dependency graph flows in one direction: Stage-specific assets may reference Common assets, but Common assets cannot hardcode references to Stage-specific assets. Therefore, any sort of ubiquitous object (like the Player or World) should remain agnostic to the stages they occupy. Let's look at the example.

The Ice Stage of the game contains new special spikes that fall from the ceiling. You created a new object: SpikeIce. Now you have to make the Player take damage and freeze when they touch it. Sounds easy!

❌ Bad:

///Player.Step
if place_meeting(x, y, SpikeIce) {
    player_take_damage()
    player_freeze()
}

Now the Player directly references SpikeIce. The analyzer will flag this, because the Player now requires the SpikeIce asset (and, therefore, all of it's referenced assets down the line, such as its sprite) to be loaded globally.

This can be solved in a few ways.

Version 1 - Moving the logic from Common to Stage-specific

Just invert the logic - make the spikes damage the player, instead of the player checking for spikes:

///IceSpike.Step
if place_meeting(x, y, Player) {
    player_take_damage()
    player_freeze()
}

This works (and is the best solution in many cases), but I bet this game has some other damage sources. How about we...

Version 2 - Turn explicit reference into implicit

... introduce a new Common object ParentHazard, and simply make the original Player logic poll for hazards, instead of specific spikes:

///Player.Step
var _hazard;
_hazard = place_meeting(x, y, ParentHazard)
if _hazard {
    player_take_damage()
    if _hazard.freeze player_freeze()
}

This is also a valid solution in many cases.

Now let's think of something less trivial. The Player now gains the ability to use spells, and the Ice Stage adds ice magic when picking up a certain powerup, implemented like this:

❌ Bad:

///Player.KeyPress_50

if global.Powerups[powerup_shield] {
    // Common spell
    instance_create(x, y, ProjectileShield)
}

if global.Powerups[powerup_spell_ice] {
    // Ice Stage spell
    instance_create_moving(x, y, ProjectileIcicle, 1, 270, 0.2)
}

You can already see the Common to Stage-specific reference.

Version 1 - Moving the logic from Common to Stage-specific

Make picking up a spell spawn an Ice Stage-bound object SpellIcicle, which houses the logic for shooting it.

///SpellIcicle.KeyPress_50
with Player {
    //handle the case when player doesn't exist (dead)
    instance_create_moving(x, y, ProjectileIcicle, 1, 270, 0.2)
}

Now the Player doesn't know about ProjectileIcicle. This solution works well for small, isolated gimmicks. However, if you want to combine the logic of several Stage-specific things, keeping a perfect dependency flow might be impossible. For such cases, we introduce...

Version 2 - Context-aware logic

Imagine now we want to assign spells to different keys and make sure the Player can't use an icicle while having a shield up or a new multistage spell "Blizzard" (existing in a cluster CommonNorth, which is accessed by both Ice Stage and Tundra Stage) is active. To punish spell abuse, you decide to add logic for Player freezing to death when spamming cold spells.

This logic can be implemented as an abstract "temperature" variable on the Player, or it can be put into a controller object. Such as ControllerSpellsNorth:

///ControllerSpellsNorth.Create
freezing = 0

///ControllerSpellsNorth.Step
//unfreeze over time
freezing = approach(freezing, 0, 0.05)

///SpellIcicle.KeyPress_50
if room_is_ice() {
    with Player {
        //spawn the icicle projectile
        instance_create_moving(x, y, ProjectileIcicle, 1, 270, 0.2)

        //lower the chill
        other.freezing -= 10

        //check if frozen
        if other.freezing < -30 {
            player_kill(killcause_freeze)
        }
    }
}

///SpellIcicle.KeyPress_51
with Player {
    //spawn the blizzard projectile
    instance_create(x, y, ProjectileBlizzard)

    other.freezing -= 20

    if other.freezing < -30 {
        player_kill(killcause_freeze)
    }
}

A few things to digest from here:

  1. ControllerSpellsNorth is now an object from CommonNorth as well - therefore it is totally allowed to reference any other asset from CommonNorth. After all, when the CommonNorth cluster is loaded, everything from it becomes available.
  2. The new function room_is_ice - is not just an ordinary "location check script". It can be used as a "Context Guard" in Clunkster's analyzer. We can assign it a target cluster that this script guards behind itself (the IceStage in our case): 
    CONTEXT_RULES: dict[str, set[str]] = {
    # guard for ice stage -specific things
    'room_is_ice': {
        'IceStage'

        # notice that we don't put any other more
        # "common" stages in here
    },

    # guard for things that are allowed in CommonNorth,
    # but don't require any more specific logic
    # (e.g. from IceStage)
    'room_is_north': {
        'CommonNorth'
    }
}
    Now everything protected by this guard can freely reference any IceStage asset.

Rooms of lean clusters (lean_clusters in the config) load exactly the assets they reach instead of whole clusters, so they can borrow from many stages without loading all of them (see ex4.7). Lint rules of such clusters list every stage they borrow from, which would make any guard of those stages pass everywhere, so in their rooms a guard only passes if it grants their own cluster, or the room by name ('room_is_ice': {'IceStage', 'rIceCameo'}).

  1. Since anything from the CommonNorth cluster should, logically, be available anywhere in IceStage, we must also define this behavior in a different config: 
    LINT_RULES: dict[str, set[str]] = {
    # common assets cannot borrow from Stage specific folders
    'Common': {'Common'},

    'IceStage': {
        # explicitly include the common cluster
        'Common',

        # include the regional common cluster
        'CommonNorth',

        # include anything from itself
        'IceStage',
    },

    # this will make any Ice Stage room load all 3 of those clusters

    # btw, default value for any cluster is a set of "Common" and
    #  the cluster itself
}
    Now everything in CommonNorth can be freely accessed by IceStage.

Tip: The attentive ones among you have likely noticed that this same trick can be applied to a World object, making it viable again. As a matter of fact, having multiple persistent controller objects is quite bad - you'll see in a bit.

Here's the sample implementation of those context guards.

///room_is_ice([room])
//Check whether the given room is from Ice Stage

var _room;
if argument_count == 0 {
    if global._clunkster_reg_mode return 1

    //optionally, if you are applying this tool onto an existing project,
    //you might want to temporarily bypass the guard, until you fix
    //all the initial bugs (ACTUALLY NOT RECOMMENDED)
    //return 1 //TEMP

    _room = room
}
else {
    _room = argument[0]
}

switch _room {
case rIceIntro:
case rIceBarrage:
    return 1
default:
    return 0
}

Notice that weird global._clunkster_reg_mode at the top. This is a secret tool that might come in handy later.

When you need a guard for things shared between several zones, you can implement it like this:

///room_is_north([room])
//Checks whether the room is a part of North stages (Ice, Tundra, etc.)

if argument_count==0 {
    if clunkster_is_reg() return 1

    //return 1 //TEMP

    //call without args
    if (
        room_is_ice() or
        room_is_tundra()
    ) return 1
}
else {
    var _room;_room=argument[0]
    if (
        room_is_ice(_room) or
        room_is_tundra(_room)
    ) return 1
}

return 0

Note: Clunkster is sensitive to exact way you call the context guards in code. Guarded region must start with a line if guard() { and end with just closing brackets on their own line }.

❌ Nope: Can't use other syntax

if room_is_nice()
{  // BAD: analyzer won't see guard opening
    nice_spell()
}  // GOOD: proper closing bracket

if room_is_polar() {  // GOOD: proper opening statemtent
    if room_is_bad() {  // GOOD: it handles indents pretty well
        message_bad()
    } else {  // BAD: analyzer won't see guard closing
        message_good()
    }
}

if (room_is_intro()) {  // BAD: analyzer won't see guard opening
    ...
}

// GOOD: everything is ok in this example
if room_is_forest() {
    music_forest()
    stuff_forest()
    john_forest()
}
else {
    // NOTE: analyzer actually doesn't do anything special in
    //  the 'else' blocks in context guards, just so you know
    john_not_forest()
}

❌ Nope: Can't use guards with parameters in scanned code

if room_is_hub(room_next(room)) { ...

❌ Nope: Can't pair them with any sort of boolean logic

if room_is_ending() and save_get('cleared') { ...

items.title: Timelines
items.text:
Convert them to switch statements.

///Obj.Create
time=0

///Obj.Step
time+=1

switch time {
case 20:
    ... //code on Step 20
    break
case 100:
    ... //code on Step 100
    break
}

items.title: State contamination via Globals and Persistence
items.text:
Now that we've handled the easy cases, let's look onto some that are less obvious (and harder to trace, since they won't get flagged in linters).

Global variables and persistent objects can cross cluster boundaries, making them vectors for dependency leaks.

❌ Bad: Passing a specific asset through a global variable or constant.

global.next_cutscene_actor = StageB_NpcFairy

If the Player enters Stage A, this reference will linger, and the analyzer won't be able to catch it. If the Player instantiates this reference in Stage A:

instance_create(x, y, global.next_cutscene_actor)

... it could potentially produce a broken stub-asset behavior if the Stage B has been unloaded.

❌ Bad: Overusing Persistence

Persistent objects act similarly to global variables. If you do something like: 

with WeatherBlizzard {
    ControllerWeather.current_weather = id
}
and then WeatherBlizzard's home cluster CommonNorth gets unloaded, you might get the same result as the previous example.

✅ Good: Pass abstract strings or enums and let a stage-specific non-persistent director object spawn the correct asset locally.

///StageB_NpcFairySpawner.Step
if global.next_cutscene_actor == "fairy" {
    instance_create(x, y, StageB_NpcFairy)
    global.next_cutscene_actor = ""
}

Don't forget to register all persistent objects in EXTRA_ROOTS: 

EXTRA_ROOTS: set[str] = {
    'World'
    # ...
}

〰️ Kinda ok: Having persistent objects with no potential instantiating references to assets that may become unloaded. Things like room transitions. Cases like this could be fine for you, but Clunkster's linters won't be able to detect oversights.

As a side note, all dependencies of each Extra Root will be merged with dependency graph of every room, so unless you wanna deal with humongous dependency graphs, keep your persistent controllers minimal. Ideally, just one World object.

items.title: Proper use of the Ignore Pragma
items.text:
We provide a pragma for ignoring files during dependency scans: //!clunkster: ignore. You should only use it on pure data registries that define metadata without instantiating objects.

❌ Bad: Skipping Your Homework

///Player.Collision_ForestLog

//eeehhh i need to convert collision with stage-specific object event
// into an End Step event + rip all that boolean logic, hide every
// call behind a guard or something ehhhh

//i dont feel like doin it :3
//!clunkster: ignore

with Player  {
    save_set_persistent("deaths", save_get("deaths") + 1)
    if global.player_skin == "knight" instance_create(x, y, Knight_BloodEmitter)
    else if instance_exists(mario_kart) instance_create(mario_kart.x, mario_kart.y+24, BloodEmitter)
    else instance_create(x, y, BloodEmitter)
    if (global.darkStage) {
        dark_gib_sound(1)
    }
    else {
        sound_play("player_death")

        // Dance specific
        if is_in_game() && !global.paused {
            if room != rDanceStage {
                camera_update()
            } else {
                dance_camera_update()
            }
        }
    }
    instance_create(0, 0, GameOver)
    instance_destroy()
}

❌ Bad: Putting instantiating references into registries (= making them impure)

///music_register()
//Register EVERY music in here
//!clunkster: ignore

music_def_begin("musStageTutorial",0.8)
    music_def_room(rTutorial,mus_autoplay)
    music_def_room(rTutorialBoss,mus_fadeout)
    music_def_room(rFinal_Respite,mus_autoplay)
music_def_end()

///World.RoomStart

//autostart music
_l_auto=dsmap(global._mus_room_auto,room)
if not is_undefined(_l_auto) {
    _s=ds_list_size(_l_auto)

    for (_i=0;_i<_s;_i+=1) {
        _snd=ds_list_find_value(_l_auto,_i)

        //BAD!!! The reference that was hidden from the linter
        // is now being passed into the instantiating function.
        // Since Clunkster has no idea that rFinal_Respite needed
        // "musTitle", it might put it into a cluster that
        // rFinal_Respite has no access too, playing you an
        // unloaded stub asset.
        // Woe be upon you.
        music_play(_snd)
    }
}

✅ Good: Make registries only define pure data and non-instantiating references.

///music_register()
//Register EVERY music in here
//!clunkster: ignore

music_def_begin("musTitle")
    music_def_volume(0.8)
    music_def_og_samplerate(44100)
    music_def_loop(31*44100 + 19422, 70*44100 + 28955)

    //instead of defining autoplay logic in registry,
    // autoplay logic can be moved into a different file
    // without the "ignore" pragma

    //but we can still keep logic like "make sure the track is
    // stopped when we enter any room other than this".
    // sound_stop(...) is not an instantiating function,
    // and will work just fine if this specific sound
    // was replaced with a stub "null.wav"
    music_def_room_allowed(rTitle, rOptions, rFinal_Respite)
music_def_end()

✅ Good: Guard instantiating registry logic.

///music_register()
//Register EVERY music in here

// notice: the ignore is gone

if room_is_tutorial_or_final() {
    //anything shared between tutorial and final stage

    music_def_begin("musStageTutorial",0.8)
        music_def_room(rTutorial,mus_autoplay)
        music_def_room(rTutorialBoss,mus_fadeout)
        music_def_room(rFinal_Respite,mus_autoplay)

        //Important: since we also violate one of our other principles
        // "Don't pass references across cluster boundaries through globals",
        // we must validate that all the rooms actually belong to the cluster
        assert(room_is_tutorial_or_final(rTutorial))
        assert(room_is_tutorial_or_final(rTutorialBoss))
        assert(room_is_tutorial_or_final(rFinal_Respite))
    music_def_end()
}

And, since this registry script runs only on game start, in order to not loose data that we've deliberately hidden behind guard (in Init room they'd all return 0...), we can introduce a little hack that doesn't ruin our cluster model.

Remember the global._clunkster_reg_mode from before? Here's our plan:

New script clunkster_init:

///clunkster_init()
global._clunkster_reg_mode = 0

//any other initialization logic might be
// autogenerated by Clunkster and added here

New script clunkster_registry_begin:

///clunkster_registry_begin()
global._clunkster_reg_mode = 1

New script clunkster_registry_end:

///clunkster_registry_end()
global._clunkster_reg_mode = 0

And here's how we will call the registries in Game Start:

clunkster_registry_begin()
    sound_register()
    music_register()
clunkster_registry_end()

And guards should intelligently silence themselves if used as context guards in registry mode, but still do proper validation if they were given an actual room:

///room_is_tutorial_or_final([room])
//Check whether the given room is from Tutorial or Final Stage

var _room;
if argument_count == 0 {
    if global._clunkster_reg_mode return 1

    _room = room
}
else {
    _room = argument[0]
}

switch _room {
case rTutorial:
case rTutorialBoss:
case rFinal_Respite:
    return 1
default:
    return 0
}

More info on them scripts can be found in the GML chapter.

items.title: Dehydration
items.text:
Following terms are used:

  • prepare: the process of stripping the asset from the project (compile step).
  • store-dry-prod: how the stripped asset is represented inside resulting prod build (invisible stubs).
  • store-dry-dev: how the stripped asset is represented inside resulting dev build (stubs that yell loudly when referenced).
  • store-wet: how the actual data is stored externally.
  • hydrate: the process of dynamically loading wet assets back into memory at runtime.
  • dehydrate: the process of unloading the assets from memory at runtime.

Backgrounds: impactful, high priority.

  • prepare: use gmcodec to generate .gmbck files.
  • store-dry-prod: transparent 2x2.
  • store-dry-dev: pink-black checkerboard with transparent padding
  • store-wet: .gmbck files.
  • hydrate: use background_replace_background to load externally.
  • dehydrate: use background_replace_background to replace back with dry stub.

Fonts: not numerous enough to be impactful, difficult.

Objects: slightly impactful, risky (and difficult).

Paths: not impactful.

Room: not impactful, risky.

Scripts: impossible to create dynamically without big rewrites.

Sprites: impactful, high priority.

  • prepare: use gmcodec to generate .gmspr files
  • store-dry-prod: transparent 2x2 with same number of frames as original.
  • store-dry-dev: pink-black checkerboard with transparent padding.
  • store-wet: .gmspr files.
  • hydrate: use sprite_replace_sprite to load externally.
  • dehydrate: use sprite_replace_sprite to replace back with dry stub.

Sounds: impactful, TODO.

External audio: impactful, high priority.

  • prepare:

    • put sounds from same cluster into their folders,
    • generate a script that loads every sound as null.wav (or buzz.wav) via sound_add_ext on game start,
    • convert ogg into compressed (level 2 or 3)
    • wav is mostly unchanged

  • store-dry-dev: gm82snd doesn't require files to be present, so we "store" them as manually initialized audio via buzz.wav for sounds and fiddlesticks.mp3 for music, in a script ran on game start (apply correct file extension).

  • store-dry-prod: same as above, except null.wav files for both.
  • store-wet: just files sitting in their external folders.
  • hydrate: run the loader script.
  • dehydrate: replace back with stubs.

items.title: Juicing
items.text:
For the Game Juicer we have to add a sort-of pre-compile step for the game. The goal is, simply put, to copy most of the project and apply dehydration to the assets that require it.

To elaborate:

  • we only do dehydration of sprites, backgrounds and external audio (builtin sounds aren't implemented yet (TODO), other asset types aren't impactful enough to bother)

  • dynamic loading of sprites and backgrounds presents us with a few game maker bugs that we need to address:

    • objects don't update their mask after mask's sprite got replaced, simple maks_index=mask_index in Room Start does the trick
    • rooms' backgrounds stretch flag is compile-time, but, since, I believe, in most projects it is not used often enough, all those rooms can just be fixed manually by hardcoding correct xscale and yscale for the backgrounds. If they are, in fact, numerous, then you could have a dynamic backgrounds resize code added into the Room Creation Code: 
      if background_width[0]>0 && background_height[0]>0 {
    background_xscale[0]=room_width/background_width[0]
    background_yscale[0]=room_height/background_height[0]
}

  • since for some games Juicing is the only way to run, builds must be fast:

    • processing tasks must support caching
    • asset dirs without processing can be linked (junctions on Windows, no admin rights needed)
    • heavy tasks (audio compression, image encoding) should be multiprocessed
    • copy tasks (numerous but IO-bound) can be put into threading

The requirements for "fast builds" are implemented in Clunkster through the system of "tasks" and "caching". Base of these is done in the library's respective pipeline abstraction (task.py, cache.py), actual implementation examples can be found in Juicer classes example.

With that said, the project building strategy becomes:

  • do an iterdir on project root

    • if element is a folder

      • if it belongs to an asset type that needs processing (smartly handle data folder)

        • generate processing/copy tasks

      • otherwise

        • check if this folder is allowed to exist in the project
        • link

    • if element is a file

      • check if this file is allowed to exist in the project
      • copy

  • execute the tasks (notice which things are tasks and which aren't)

    • multiprocessing for processing tasks (image encoding, audio compression)
    • threading for copy tasks

Speaking of building, one more note on how the built game is structured. By default, wet assets are stored in data/chunks/<cluster>/<whatever was their original path relative to the project root>.

items.title: Pipeline architecture
items.text:
The library is split from the pipeline on purpose: the library (clunkster package) does the GameMaker-specific heavy lifting and returns data, while the pipeline (main.py) decides how things are configured, printed and run. The library never prints, raises on linter errors or picks a UI; it has no dependencies beyond the ones its parsers need.

Pipeline systems live in the pipeline folder:

  • task.py: Task encapsulates information needed for processing logic, input and output files for build caching, and houses the execute method that actually does the thing.
  • cache.py: The build cache, saved into a JSON file. Tasks whose output files are present and whose input files haven't changed are skipped. Input files are compared by their stats (modification time, size, file id) first, and only hashed when those changed, so builds don't read every input every time.
  • run.py: Task execution. tasks_filter_stale drops tasks that are fresh in the cache, tasks_run executes the rest in a given concurrent.futures pool (threads for IO-bound copies, processes for CPU-bound encoding) and records successes in the cache. Progress is reported through an optional callback, called in the main thread after each task with the worker that ran it and the tasks running right now (taken from the pool's futures), so workers don't need to communicate anything beyond their results. The examples use it for a live view of what each worker does.

Reference scanning results are cached per file (see analyze/scan_cache.py): a file is only rescanned when its stats or the set of asset names change. This keeps repeated checks and the watch mode fast.

Linting follows the same idea (see lint.py): checks are Rules, problems are Violations collected into plain lists, and format_report turns them into text. Printing the report and raising on errors is up to the pipeline.

Output in the examples goes through rich: status messages via logging, progress bars via progress, and step headers via the step decorator (see ex0.2).

Full example of a synchronous pipeline step can be found here: ex0.3.

Full example of running tasks concurrently can be found here: ex4.2.

items.title: Integration into the game
items.text:
In order to integrate Clunkster into your project you'll have to create a couple of GML scripts. Some of them will be autogenerated in Game Juicer and its derivatives. The game gets a table of every dehydrated asset and, for every room, a list of the assets it needs. Loading is done when the room change is requested (in room_goto): assets of the target room that aren't loaded yet get loaded. Unloading is done in the Room Start event: assets no room needed for more than keep_rooms room changes (1 by default, so going back to the previous room is free) get replaced by stubs. This results in stutters when changing to rooms with a lot of new assets, which I'd imagine won't be an issue, especially if such room changes have transitions like black-out-black-in.

What a room needs depends on the build: every dehydrated asset of the room's clusters, or, in lean builds (ex4.7), exactly what the room uses.

Here's the static scripts that you'll have to add:

  • clunkster_init(): Initializes Clunkster's variables and asset tables.
  • clunkster_room_start(): Clunkster's Room Start event, unloads assets that are no longer needed.
  • clunkster_room_goto(target_room): A room_goto replacement that ensures all assets are loaded for target room.
  • clunkster_hydrate(asset): Loads an asset from the table.
  • clunkster_dehydrate(asset): Unloads an asset from the table (replaces it with a dry stub to reduce RAM).
  • clunkster_init_audio(): Initializes audio stubs.
  • clunkster_registry_begin(): Toggles registry mode on.
  • clunkster_is_reg(): Returns registry mode status.
  • clunkster_registry_end(): Toggles registry mode off.

And the following scripts will be autogenerated. You should still add them - their contents are populated in the GML generation step: ex4.3. In raw project those are usually empty.

  • clunkster_gen_type(): Returns "dev" or "prod" in a built project. Returns "" in the raw source project.
  • clunkster_gen_init(): Fills the asset tables and room lists.
  • clunkster_gen_validate_ctx(): Validation script that runs on Game Start and checks that context guards correctly guard their rooms. A guard failing in a room of its clusters is an error, a guard passing in a room where the dependency graphs assumed it doesn't (so assets behind it aren't loaded there) is a warning.

Following describes the base implementation of those scripts, as well as notes on what kinds of changes should be made to the project in order for these to work.

  1. clunkster_init() - Initializes Clunkster logic

    ///clunkster_init()
//Initialize clunkster globals and asset tables

global.__clunk_reg_mode=0
//room -> ds_list of assets (indices into the tables) the room needs
global.__clunk_rooms=ds_map_create()
//room changes so far, and how many an asset stays loaded for after its last room
global.__clunk_tick=0
global.__clunk_keep=1
global.__clunk_count=0
clunkster_gen_init()

//room change each asset was last needed at, -1 while it's not loaded
var _i;
for (_i=0;_i<global.__clunk_count;_i+=1) global.__clunk_last[_i]=-1

clunkster_gen_validate_ctx()

    See example of proper Game Start logic below.

  2. clunkster_room_start() - System's Room Start event, responsible for unloading assets.

    ///clunkster_room_start()
//Clunkster's Room Start event
//Unload assets that no room needed for more than global.__clunk_keep room changes

var _i;
for (_i=0;_i<global.__clunk_count;_i+=1) {
    if global.__clunk_last[_i]>=0 and global.__clunk_last[_i]<global.__clunk_tick-global.__clunk_keep {
        clunkster_dehydrate(_i)
        global.__clunk_last[_i]=-1
    }
}

    Put it in World's Room Start at the top.

  3. clunkster_room_goto(target_room) - Interceptor of room_goto calls, which is responsible for loading any asset required by target room.

    ///clunkster_room_goto(room)
//Intercept room_goto and load assets the room needs

var _l,_i,_a;
global.__clunk_tick+=1
if ds_map_exists(global.__clunk_rooms,argument0) {
    _l=ds_map_find_value(global.__clunk_rooms,argument0)
    for (_i=0;_i<ds_list_size(_l);_i+=1) {
        _a=ds_list_find_value(_l,_i)
        if global.__clunk_last[_a]<0 clunkster_hydrate(_a)
        global.__clunk_last[_a]=global.__clunk_tick
    }
}

room_goto(argument0)

    You'll have to replace every room_goto call with this function, and never use any other methods of room change.

  4. clunkster_hydrate(asset) - Load an asset from its wet file.

    ///clunkster_hydrate(asset)
//Load an asset (index into clunkster tables) from its wet file

var _r,_f;
_r=global.__clunk_res[argument0]
_f=global.__clunk_file[argument0]
switch global.__clunk_kind[argument0] {
case 0:
    sprite_replace_sprite(_r,_f)
    break
case 1:
    background_replace_background(_r,_f)
    break
case 2:
    sound_replace(_r,_f,global.__clunk_skind[argument0],global.__clunk_pre[argument0])
    sndreg_apply(_r)
    break
}

    sndreg_apply applies the sound registry, see below.

  5. clunkster_dehydrate(asset) - Unload an asset, replacing it with its stub.

    ///clunkster_dehydrate(asset)
//Unload an asset (index into clunkster tables), replacing it with its stub

var _r;
_r=global.__clunk_res[argument0]
switch global.__clunk_kind[argument0] {
case 0:
    sprite_replace_sprite(_r,global.__clunk_stub_spr)
    break
case 1:
    background_replace_background(_r,global.__clunk_stub_bg)
    break
case 2:
    sound_replace(_r,global.__clunk_stub[argument0],global.__clunk_skind[argument0],global.__clunk_pre[argument0])
    break
}

  6. clunkster_init_audio() - Add dehydrated audio as stubs.

    ///clunkster_init_audio()
//Add dehydrated audio as stubs, so it can be played and loaded by name
//Call after the sound registry is populated

var _i;
for (_i=0;_i<global.__clunk_count;_i+=1) {
    if global.__clunk_kind[_i]==2 {
        sound_add_ext(global.__clunk_stub[_i],global.__clunk_skind[_i],global.__clunk_stream[_i],global.__clunk_res[_i])
    }
}

    Next are registry-related functions.

  7. clunkster_registry_begin() - Switch registry mode ON.

    ///clunkster_registry_begin()

global.__clunk_reg_mode=1

  8. clunkster_registry_end() - Switch registry mode OFF.

    ///clunkster_registry_end()

global.__clunk_reg_mode=0

  9. clunkster_is_reg() - Check whether in registry mode.

    ///clunkster_is_reg()
//Check whether in registry mode

return global.__clunk_reg_mode

    And finally, the autogenerated scripts. In raw project they remain mostly empty.

  10. clunkster_gen_type()

    ///clunkster_gen_type()
//Returns the type of project.
//Expect "dev" for builds with no dynamic asset loading
//Expect "prod" for builds with dynamic asset loading
//Expect "" for raw projects

//This script is autogenerated by Clunkster.

return ""

  11. clunkster_gen_init()

    ///clunkster_gen_init()
//Fill asset tables of the build: per asset global.__clunk_kind (0 sprite,
// 1 background, 2 sound), global.__clunk_res, global.__clunk_file (and for
// sounds global.__clunk_skind/stream/pre/stub), plus global.__clunk_count,
// global.__clunk_keep, stubs and global.__clunk_rooms

//This script is autogenerated by Clunkster.

  12. clunkster_gen_validate_ctx()

    ///clunkster_gen_validate_ctx()
//Validate room context guards

//This script is autogenerated by Clunkster.

What are the registries? Basically, if you wanna have some values associated with a externalized resource, that should be applied whenever its loaded, you can simply put such data in a dsmap and add some logic for loading and applying those values.

For example, if you have some values associated with audio source (like volume balancing, original sample rate, loops), you can create a registry, like this sndreg:

sndreg_init:

///sndreg_init()
//Initialize sound registry

global._sndreg=ds_map_create()
global._sndlist=ds_list_create()

sndreg_ext - Fills in all data of an audio at once:

///sndreg_ext(snd,og_samplerate=44100,vol=1,[loopstart,loopend=-1])
//Fill in all params at once

//reg
if !ds_map_exists(global._sndreg,argument0+":REG") {
    ds_list_add(global._sndlist,argument0)
    dsmap(global._sndreg,argument0+":REG",1)
}

//rate
//NOTE: I recommend avoiding unit_samples and unit_seconds, as FMOD's
// native format is unit_unitary
var _rate;if argument_count>1 _rate=argument[1] else _rate=44100
dsmap(global._sndreg,argument0+":RATE",_rate)

//vol
var _vol;if argument_count>2 _vol=argument[2] else _vol=1
dsmap(global._sndreg,argument0+":VOL",_vol)

//loop
if argument_count>3 {
    dsmap(global._sndreg,argument0+":LA",argument[3])
    var _le;
    if argument_count>4 _le=argument[4] else _le=-1
    dsmap(global._sndreg,argument0+":LB",_le)
}

sndreg_populate - This is where you define all those values:

///sndreg_populate()
//Populate sound registry with necessary sound data

sndreg_ext("block_break",44100)
sndreg_ext("block_change",44100,0.8)
sndreg_ext("boss_hit",44100,0.8)
sndreg_ext("cherry_trap",44100,0.6)
sndreg_ext("get_item",44100)
sndreg_ext("glass",44100)

if room_is_ice_stage() {
    sndreg_ext("ice_melt",44100)
}

sndreg_apply - Apply registry values to a sound:

///sndreg_apply(snd)
if sound_exists(argument0) {
    //volume
    var _vol;_vol=dsmap(global._sndreg,argument0+":VOL")
    if is_undefined(_vol) _vol=1
    sound_volume(argument0,_vol)

    //loop
    var _ls;_ls=dsmap(global._sndreg,argument0+":LA")
    if not is_undefined(_ls) {
        var _le;_le=dsmap(global._sndreg,argument0+":LB")
        if is_undefined(_le) _le=-1

        //scale samplerate to account for compression
        var _scaled_start,_scaled_end;
        _scaled_start=sndreg_scale_sample(argument0,_ls)

        if _le==-1 {
            _scaled_end=sound_get_length(argument0,unit_samples)
        }
        else {
            _scaled_end=sndreg_scale_sample(argument0,_le)
        }
        sound_set_loop(
            argument0,
            _scaled_start,_scaled_end,unit_samples
        )
    }
}
else {
    show_error(str_ins(
        "sndreg_apply: Sound '%' doesn't exist",argument0
    ),0)
}

sndreg_apply_all - Apply registry values to all registered sounds; this one should be used right after registry population, if project type is raw.

///sndreg_apply_all()
//Apply audio stuff to all sounds

var _i,_ac,_snd;
_ac=ds_list_size(global._sndlist)
for (_i=0;_i<_ac;_i+=1) {
    _snd=ds_list_find_value(global._sndlist,_i)
    sndreg_apply(_snd)
}

This allows us to write a clean Game Start logic:

clunkster_registry_begin()
sndreg_populate()
clunkster_registry_end()
if clunkster_gen_type() == "" {
    //all audio is internal and loaded, run audio balance
    sndreg_apply_all()
}
else {
    //we are in 'dev' or 'prod' build, generate stubs
    clunkster_init_audio()
}

items.title: Examples
items.text: Examples are generated from the main pipeline file, and represent parts of the workflow for the game this tool was initially build for. The game structure is Verve GM8.2 Engine for IWBTG fangames, though changing that should be easy.

items.title: 0 - Setting up
items.text:
This is the setup section. It covers settings up the project, linters, and other pipeline shims. Of these, mandatory ones are:

  • Config
  • Output

items.title: Example 0.1 - Setup: Config
items.text:
Set up the configuration.

There's no global state: every pipeline step receives Config as its first argument. It holds:

  • project: source project root (where game's .gm82 file is stored), also caches file reads
  • alias, lint_rules, context_rules, extra_roots: cluster setup, explained in the examples that use them
  • juicer: Game Juicer settings
import dataclasses
from pathlib import Path

from clunkster import project as my_proj

@dataclasses.dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class Config:
    """Pipeline configuration, passed into every pipeline step."""

    # source project (root, where game's .gm82 file is stored + file reads)
    project: my_proj.Project
    # cluster name -> top level folders merged into it (see ALIAS)
    alias: dict[str, list[str]]
    # cluster -> clusters it may reference (see LINT_RULES)
    lint_rules: dict[str, set[str]]
    # guard script -> clusters (and rooms of lean clusters) it grants (see
    #  CONTEXT_RULES)
    context_rules: dict[str, set[str]]
    # persistent objects present in every room (see EXTRA_ROOTS)
    extra_roots: set[str]
    # Game Juicer settings (see JUICER)
    juicer: ConfJuicer
    # reference scan cache file
    scan_cache: Path
    # RAM budget (MB) for assets moved to Common because of cluster violations
    common_budget_mb: float = 500
    # terms that shouldn't be used anymore (assets, scripts, functions) ->
    #  why, see main_ex_lint_blacklist
    blacklist: dict[str, str] = dataclasses.field(default_factory=dict)
    # clusters whose rooms load exactly the assets they reach instead of
    #  whole clusters (see main_ex_lean)
    lean_clusters: frozenset[str] = frozenset()
    # context guards that pass anywhere on purpose (shims silencing the
    #  compiler), no warnings about them passing outside their rules
    context_shims: frozenset[str] = frozenset()
    # assets moved to Common because of cluster violations, derived by the
    #  cluster checks (see main_ex_promote_refs)
    promoted: frozenset[str] = frozenset()
    # lean builds: assets kept in the executable, derived by main_ex_lean
    #  (None: Common assets are)
    resident: frozenset[str] | None = None
    # top level folder -> cluster name, derived from alias
    alias_inv: dict[str, str] = dataclasses.field(init=False)

    def __post_init__(self) -> None:
        """Derive ``alias_inv`` from ``alias``."""
        alias_inv: dict[str, str] = {}
        for name, clusters in self.alias.items():
            for cluster in clusters:
                if cluster in alias_inv:
                    raise ValueError(f"Invalid alias (duplicate: '{cluster}')")
                alias_inv[cluster] = name
        object.__setattr__(self, 'alias_inv', alias_inv)

cfg = Config(
    # project root must be absolute
    project=my_proj.Project(Path('path/to/the/project').resolve()),
    alias=ALIAS,
    lint_rules=LINT_RULES,
    context_rules=CONTEXT_RULES,
    extra_roots=EXTRA_ROOTS,
    juicer=JUICER,
    scan_cache=Path(__file__).parent / 'scan_cache.json',
)

Values for the rest of the fields are introduced in the examples that need them.

items.title: Example 0.2 - Setup: Output
items.text:
Set up the output.

Pipeline steps don't print directly: status messages go through logging, sequences get progress bars via progress, and the step decorator marks where a step starts and how long it took. All of it goes through rich, which falls back to plain text when the output isn't a terminal.

import collections.abc as col
import functools as ft
import logging
import sys
import time

from rich import console as r_console
from rich import progress as r_progress
from rich import table as r_table
from rich.logging import RichHandler

# rich falls back to 80 columns when not printing into a terminal (IDE
#  consoles, logs), which is too narrow for some tables
CONSOLE = r_console.Console(width=None if sys.stdout.isatty() else 160)
log = logging.getLogger('clunkster')


def setup_output() -> None:
    """Route logging and warnings through the console."""
    logging.basicConfig(
        level=logging.INFO,
        format='%(message)s',
        handlers=[
            RichHandler(
                console=CONSOLE,
                show_time=False,
                show_level=False,
                show_path=False,
            )
        ],
    )
    logging.captureWarnings(capture=True)


def step[**P, R](
    name: str,
) -> col.Callable[[col.Callable[P, R]], col.Callable[P, R]]:
    """Pipeline step decorator: prints a header and how long the step took."""

    def decorator(func: col.Callable[P, R]) -> col.Callable[P, R]:
        @ft.wraps(func)
        def wrapper(*args: P.args, **kwargs: P.kwargs) -> R:
            CONSOLE.rule(name)
            start = time.perf_counter()
            result = func(*args, **kwargs)
            log.info('%s: done in %.2fs', name, time.perf_counter() - start)
            return result

        return wrapper

    return decorator


def progress[T](
    seq: col.Sequence[T], description: str = 'Working'
) -> col.Iterator[T]:
    """Iterate over a sequence while showing a progress bar."""
    # updating the bar is not free, so do it at most ~1000 times
    update_every = max(1, len(seq) // 1000)
    with r_progress.Progress(console=CONSOLE, transient=True) as bar:
        bar_task = bar.add_task(description, total=len(seq))
        for idx, item in enumerate(seq, start=1):
            yield item
            if idx % update_every == 0:
                bar.update(bar_task, completed=idx)


def render_table(
    table: col.Sequence[col.Sequence[str]], *, title: str | None = None
) -> None:
    """Print a 2D sequence of strings, ``table[0]`` contains the headers."""
    if len(table) < 2:
        return
    headers = table[0]
    rich_table = r_table.Table(
        f'[bold]{headers[0]}[/bold]', *headers[1:], title=title, padding=0
    )
    for row in table[1:]:
        rich_table.add_row(*row)
    CONSOLE.print(rich_table)

setup_output()

With that out of the way you may start the first real examples. However, I recommend reading a bit about the pipeline architecture, which should give you proper understanding on what to do if things don't work out.

items.title: Example 0.3 - Full example (pipeline excerpt)
items.text:
Following is the full example of a pipeline step with output, taken from main.py (where you can look for more thorough examples as well).

import logging
import time

from rich import console as r_console

# see ex0.2 - Setup: Output
CONSOLE: r_console.Console = ...
log: logging.Logger = ...
def setup_output(): ...
def step(): ...
def progress(): ...
def render_table(): ...

@step('Example step')
def main_example() -> None:
    """Example pipeline step."""
    log.info('Good weather up there')
    time.sleep(1)
    log.info('Makes me forget about my job: counting to 10')
    for number in progress(range(10), 'Counting'):
        time.sleep(0.5)
        log.info('Number %d', number)
    log.info('Clear?!! No way')

items.title: 1 - Reading project
items.text: This section is about discovering assets from project files, doing initial validations and assigning clusters to the assets.

items.title: Example 1.1 - Finding assets
items.text:
Let's start with some simple scanning.

Clunkster already provides utils for scanning builtin assets and single-file external assets (such as audio for gm82snd). However, registering those external assets is left as a task for the user.

import collections.abc as col
import dataclasses
from abc import ABC
from pathlib import Path
from typing import override

from clunkster import asset as my_asset
from clunkster.asset import Asset

# see ex0.1 - Setup: Config
class Config: ...

@dataclasses.dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class AssetExtAudio(my_asset.AssetSingleFile, ABC):
    """Generic external audio asset."""


@dataclasses.dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class AssetExtBgm(AssetExtAudio):
    """External background music asset."""

    @override
    @classmethod
    def type_name(cls) -> str:
        return 'DATA_BGM'

    @override
    @classmethod
    def type_globs(cls) -> tuple[str, ...]:
        return '*.ogg', '*.mp3', '*.wav'

    @override
    @classmethod
    def type_get_dir_rel(cls) -> Path:
        return Path('data') / 'music'


@dataclasses.dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class AssetExtSfx(AssetExtAudio):
    """External sound effect asset (kind 0)."""

    @override
    @classmethod
    def type_name(cls) -> str:
        return 'DATA_SFX'

    @override
    @classmethod
    def type_globs(cls) -> col.Iterable[str]:
        return ('*.wav',)

    @override
    @classmethod
    def type_get_dir_rel(cls) -> Path:
        return Path('data') / 'sounds'


@dataclasses.dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class AssetExtSfx3(AssetExtAudio):
    """External sound effect asset (kind 3)."""

    @override
    @classmethod
    def type_name(cls) -> str:
        return 'DATA_SFX3'

    @override
    @classmethod
    def type_globs(cls) -> col.Iterable[str]:
        return '*.ogg', '*.mp3'

    @override
    @classmethod
    def type_get_dir_rel(cls) -> Path:
        return Path('data') / 'sounds'

CLUSTERABLE_ASSETS: tuple[type[my_asset.AssetHasPath], ...] = (
    my_asset.Sprite,
    my_asset.Background,
    my_asset.Sound,
    my_asset.Path,
    my_asset.Script,
    my_asset.Font,
    my_asset.Object,
    my_asset.Room,
    AssetExtBgm,
    AssetExtSfx,
    AssetExtSfx3,
)

assets: list[Asset] = []

for asset_type in CLUSTERABLE_ASSETS:
    # check if given asset type exist in the project
    if not asset_type.type_is_used(cfg.project.root):
        continue

    # type_discover_all handles the discovery of all assets per
    #  asset type.
    assets.extend(asset_type.type_discover_all(cfg.project.root))

print(f'Discovered {len(assets)} total assets.')

I recommend checking the resulting assets array for any weirdness in debug before going further.

items.title: Example 1.2 - Lint: tree.yyd files
items.text:
Now we must check integrity of tree.yyd files and asset names.

Asset discovery and clusterization is based on scanning tree.yyd files, so we have to ensure that they have no duplicate folders.

This example also serves as an introduction to Clunkster's linter system. Each check is a Rule (code like T100, title and severity), and each problem found is a Violation of a rule. Violations optionally carry a message, a location in a file, an asset, a group (used to group the report, e.g. by cluster) and extra detail lines. Steps collect them into a list and pass it to lint_report, which prints the report (grouped by rule, sorted by asset and location) and raises if any of the violations is an error.

For linting tree.yyd files we want to check that:

  1. all asset names are unique (T101): not bound to a specific file, since duplicate assets can exist across multiple types.
  2. no duplicate folders in tree (T100): checked within same asset type and bound to a location in specific tree.yyd file.

Since any inconsistency in asset structure will cause big issues in the pipeline, both rules are errors.

import collections
import collections.abc as col

from clunkster import asset as my_asset
from clunkster import lint as my_lint
from clunkster.parse import tree as my_parse_tree
from clunkster.text import location as my_location

# see ex0.1 - Setup: Config
class Config: ...

# see ex1.1 - Finding assets
class AssetExtAudio: ...
class AssetExtBgm: ...
class AssetExtSfx: ...
class AssetExtSfx3: ...

def lint_report(
    cfg: Config, violations: col.Sequence[my_lint.Violation]
) -> None:
    """Print violations, raise if any of them is an error."""
    if not violations:
        return
    CONSOLE.print(
        my_lint.format_report(violations, cfg.project),
        markup=False,
        highlight=False,
        soft_wrap=True,
    )
    errors = [
        v for v in violations if v.rule.severity == my_lint.Severity.ERROR
    ]
    if errors:
        raise my_lint.LinterFoundError(
            f'Linter found {len(errors)} error(s)', errors
        )

RULE_TREE_DUPLICATE_FOLDER = my_lint.Rule(
    'T100', 'duplicate tree.yyd folder', my_lint.Severity.ERROR
)
RULE_TREE_DUPLICATE_ASSET = my_lint.Rule(
    'T101', 'duplicate asset name', my_lint.Severity.ERROR
)

CLUSTERABLE_ASSETS: tuple[type[my_asset.AssetHasPath], ...] = (
    my_asset.Sprite,
    my_asset.Background,
    my_asset.Sound,
    my_asset.Path,
    my_asset.Script,
    my_asset.Font,
    my_asset.Object,
    my_asset.Room,
    AssetExtBgm,
    AssetExtSfx,
    AssetExtSfx3,
)

# check that there are no duplicates
violations: list[my_lint.Violation] = []
asset_names: set[str] = set()
for asset_type in CLUSTERABLE_ASSETS:
    # check if given asset type exist in the project
    if not asset_type.type_is_used(cfg.project.root):
        continue

    # populate namespace
    assets_from_index = list(
        asset_type.type_discover_names(cfg.project.root)
    )
    assets_set = set(assets_from_index)
    dupes = [
        item
        for item, count in collections.Counter(assets_from_index).items()
        if count > 1
    ]
    if dupes:
        violations.append(
            my_lint.Violation(
                RULE_TREE_DUPLICATE_ASSET,
                f'Duplicate assets in one type: {" ".join(dupes)}',
            )
        )
    inters = asset_names.intersection(assets_set)
    if inters:
        violations.append(
            my_lint.Violation(
                RULE_TREE_DUPLICATE_ASSET,
                'Duplicate assets across multiple types: '
                + ' '.join(sorted(inters)),
            )
        )
    asset_names.update(assets_set)

# report before parsing tree.yyd
lint_report(cfg, violations)

# check tree.yyd files of builtin assets
violations = []
for asset_type in CLUSTERABLE_ASSETS:
    if not issubclass(asset_type, my_asset.AssetBuiltin):
        continue
    if not asset_type.type_is_used(cfg.project.root):
        continue

    tree_file = asset_type.type_get_tree_file(cfg.project.root)
    line_map = cfg.project.line_map(tree_file)
    seen_children: dict[str, set[str]] = {}

    for node in my_parse_tree.nodes(cfg.project.lines(tree_file)):
        # format the tuple into path string (e.g., "/Player/SkinA")
        path_str = '/' + '/'.join(node.parent_path)
        seen = seen_children.setdefault(path_str, set())

        if node.name not in seen:
            seen.add(node.name)
            continue

        loc_line = node.line_num
        loc_column = node.depth + 1  # uses tab characters
        thing = 'Folder' if node.is_folder else 'Asset???'
        violations.append(
            my_lint.Violation(
                RULE_TREE_DUPLICATE_FOLDER,
                f"Duplicate {thing}: '{node.name}'",
                location=my_location.Location(
                    file=tree_file,
                    loc_line=loc_line,
                    loc_column=loc_column,
                    loc_index=line_map.get_abs_index(loc_line, loc_column),
                ),
            )
        )

lint_report(cfg, violations)

items.title: Example 1.3 - Clusters
items.text:
Generate clusters.

Once we validated assets and trees, we can do cluster generation. We'll look at the top level folder name. In order to merge things like "StageA" and "stage_a" into single cluster "StageA", we'll use the alias system.

Now, the alias dictionary can become quite large, so I added additional validation. Now we detect unused or extra names.

Also, this script has a neat table output for clusters per asset type, It can be useful to discern where exactly any extra names are located.

import logging

from rich import console as r_console

from clunkster import asset as my_asset
from clunkster import lint as my_lint
from clunkster.asset import Asset

# see ex0.1 - Setup: Config
class Config: ...

# see ex0.2 - Setup: Output
CONSOLE: r_console.Console = ...
log: logging.Logger = ...
def setup_output(): ...
def step(): ...
def progress(): ...
def render_table(): ...

# see ex1.2 - Lint: `tree.yyd` files
def lint_report(): ...

# see ex1.1 - Finding assets
class AssetExtAudio: ...
class AssetExtBgm: ...
class AssetExtSfx: ...
class AssetExtSfx3: ...

ALIAS: dict[str, list[str]] = {
    'StageA': [
        'stage_a',
        'stageA',
        'StageA Music',
        # ...
    ],
    'StageB': [
        'objStageB',
        'rStageB',
        # ...
    ],
    'Common': [
        'Backgrounds',
        'Blocks',
        'Default',
        # ...
    ],
    # ...
}

def asset_cluster_raw(asset: my_asset.AssetHasPath) -> str:
    """Get asset's initial cluster before aliasing."""
    return asset.tree_path[0] if asset.tree_path else 'Common'


def asset_cluster(cfg: Config, asset: my_asset.Asset) -> str:
    """Get asset's cluster."""
    if asset.name in cfg.promoted:
        return 'Common'
    if isinstance(asset, my_asset.AssetHasPath):
        cluster = asset_cluster_raw(asset)
        alias = cfg.alias_inv.get(cluster)
        return cluster if alias is None else alias
    return 'Unknown?'

RULE_ALIAS_MISMATCH = my_lint.Rule(
    'A100', 'alias mismatch', my_lint.Severity.WARNING
)

CLUSTERABLE_ASSETS: tuple[type[my_asset.AssetHasPath], ...] = (
    my_asset.Sprite,
    my_asset.Background,
    my_asset.Sound,
    my_asset.Path,
    my_asset.Script,
    my_asset.Font,
    my_asset.Object,
    my_asset.Room,
    AssetExtBgm,
    AssetExtSfx,
    AssetExtSfx3,
)

assets: list[Asset] = []

# ALIAS linter: find existing names in ALIAS
lint_existing_aliases: set[str] = set()
for name, clusters in cfg.alias.items():
    for cluster in clusters:
        lint_existing_aliases.add(cluster)
        lint_existing_aliases.add(name)

# this will help us generate the table below
table_type_to_clusters: dict[type[Asset], list[str]] = {}

# ALIAS linter: find actually used names in ALIAS
lint_used_aliases: set[str] = set()
for asset_type in CLUSTERABLE_ASSETS:
    if not asset_type.type_is_used(cfg.project.root):
        continue

    cluster_set: set[str] = set()
    for asset in asset_type.type_discover_all(cfg.project.root):
        # add both generated cluster and its alias
        cluster = asset_cluster(cfg, asset)
        lint_used_aliases.add(asset_cluster_raw(asset))
        lint_used_aliases.add(cluster)

        cluster_set.add(cluster)

        assets.append(asset)

    table_type_to_clusters[asset_type] = list(cluster_set)

# generate the table
clusters_all = {
    name
    for clusters in table_type_to_clusters.values()
    for name in clusters
}
clusters_all_sorted = sorted(clusters_all)
asset_types = list(table_type_to_clusters.keys())
table: list[list[str]] = [
    ['Cluster', *(at.type_name() for at in asset_types)]
]

# 3. Add rows: One row per cluster
for cluster_name in clusters_all_sorted:
    row = [cluster_name]

    for asset_type in asset_types:
        if cluster_name in table_type_to_clusters[asset_type]:
            row.append(asset_type.type_name())
        else:
            row.append('')

    table.append(row)

render_table(table, title='Clusters')

# lint
lint_unused_aliases = lint_existing_aliases - lint_used_aliases
lint_extra_aliases = lint_used_aliases - lint_existing_aliases
violations: list[my_lint.Violation] = []
if lint_unused_aliases:
    violations.append(
        my_lint.Violation(
            RULE_ALIAS_MISMATCH,
            f'Unused aliases: {" ".join(sorted(lint_unused_aliases))}',
        )
    )
if lint_extra_aliases:
    # after the initial project setup, I'd upgrade this to raise
    violations.append(
        my_lint.Violation(
            RULE_ALIAS_MISMATCH,
            f'Extra aliases: {" ".join(sorted(lint_extra_aliases))}',
        )
    )
lint_report(cfg, violations)

Keep using the table thing until all aliases are gone.

items.title: 2 - References
items.text: This section is about finding asset references in .gml files, and running validations based on them.

items.title: Example 2.1 - Reference scanning
items.text:
Reference scanner.

In order to run dependency linters, we need to scan the actual references. We'll use pyahocorasick library to make it decently fast.

Text occurrences found like this reflect occurrences in static code, but with some exceptions (strings, comments). Filtering through such is implemented in Clunkster.

Also, for pure data registry scripts (like sound_balance), which, technically reference every asset, but don't instantiate them, we added a special directive: //!clunkster: ignore. Add it in any GML scripts that should be skipped.

Scanning every file on every run is slow-ish, so results are cached per file in ScanCache, and only files whose stat changed are rescanned. Changing the set of asset names (e.g. adding an asset) rescans everything, in parallel. Saving the cache is left to the caller.

Blacklisted terms (see main_ex_lint_blacklist) are searched for in the same pass.

import collections.abc as col
import concurrent.futures
import dataclasses
import hashlib
from pathlib import Path

from ahocorasick import Automaton

from clunkster import asset as my_asset
from clunkster.analyze import scan_cache as my_scan_cache
from clunkster.analyze import scan_dep as my_scan_dep
from clunkster.asset import Asset
from clunkster.pipeline import task as my_task
from clunkster.text import location as my_location
from clunkster.text.line import LineMap

# see ex0.1 - Setup: Config
class Config: ...

# see ex1.1 - Finding assets
class AssetExtAudio: ...
class AssetExtBgm: ...
class AssetExtSfx: ...
class AssetExtSfx3: ...

# see ex1.3 - Clusters
def asset_cluster_raw(): ...
def asset_cluster(): ...

def asset_scannables(asset: Asset, project_root: Path) -> col.Iterable[Path]:
    """Get asset's scannable code files."""
    if isinstance(asset, my_asset.Object):
        yield asset.get_object_metadata_file(project_root)
        yield asset.get_object_gml_file(project_root)
    elif isinstance(asset, my_asset.Room):
        # easier to rglob
        dir_room = asset.get_room_folder(project_root)
        yield from dir_room.rglob('*.txt')
        yield from dir_room.rglob('*.gml')
    elif isinstance(asset, my_asset.Script):
        yield asset.get_script_gml_file(project_root)
    # add finders for new asset types

@dataclasses.dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class Dependency:
    """Full dependency data to be used in graph building."""

    location: my_location.Location
    source_asset: my_asset.Asset
    target_asset: my_asset.Asset
    contexts: tuple[str, ...]

@dataclasses.dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class TermUse:
    """Use of a blacklisted term."""

    term: str
    location: my_location.Location
    source_asset: Asset

# scanning more files than this is done in a process pool
SCAN_POOL_MIN_FILES = 500

# automaton of the scanning process, see _scan_init
_SCAN_AUTOMATON: Automaton | None = None


def _scan_init(names: col.Iterable[str]) -> None:
    """Build the automaton for searching names (once per process)."""
    global _SCAN_AUTOMATON
    _SCAN_AUTOMATON = Automaton()
    for name in names:
        _SCAN_AUTOMATON.add_word(name, name)
    _SCAN_AUTOMATON.make_automaton()


def _scan_file(file: Path) -> tuple[my_scan_cache.FileMatch, ...]:
    """Find references in a file."""
    assert _SCAN_AUTOMATON is not None, 'call _scan_init first'
    text = file.read_text(encoding='utf-8')
    line_map = LineMap.from_text(text)
    return tuple(
        my_scan_cache.FileMatch(
            match.idx,
            *line_map.get_line_col(match.idx),
            match.target,
            match.contexts,
        )
        for match in my_scan_dep.scan(text, _SCAN_AUTOMATON.iter(text))
    )


def scan_files(
    names: col.Sequence[str], files: col.Sequence[Path]
) -> list[tuple[my_scan_cache.FileMatch, ...]]:
    """Find references to given names in files, return matches per file."""
    if len(files) < SCAN_POOL_MIN_FILES:
        _scan_init(names)
        return [_scan_file(file) for file in progress(files, 'Scanning')]
    with concurrent.futures.ProcessPoolExecutor(
        initializer=_scan_init, initargs=(names,)
    ) as pool:
        return list(pool.map(_scan_file, files, chunksize=64))

# see ex1.3 - Clusters
assets: list[Asset] = ...

names = sorted({asset.name for asset in assets} | cfg.blacklist.keys())
scan_cache.set_names(
    hashlib.md5('\n'.join(names).encode('utf-8')).hexdigest()
)

scans = tuple(
    (asset, file_path)
    for asset in assets
    for file_path in asset_scannables(asset, cfg.project.root)
)

# look up cached matches, stat files before reading them
file_matches: dict[Path, tuple[my_scan_cache.FileMatch, ...]] = {}
stale: list[tuple[Path, my_task.FileStat]] = []
for _, file_path in scans:
    stat = my_task.file_stat(file_path)
    matches = scan_cache.get(file_path, stat)
    if matches is None:
        stale.append((file_path, stat))
    else:
        file_matches[file_path] = matches
log.info('%d file(s) cached, %d to scan', len(file_matches), len(stale))

stale_files = [file_path for file_path, _ in stale]
for (file_path, stat), matches in zip(
    stale, scan_files(names, stale_files), strict=True
):
    scan_cache.put(file_path, stat, matches)
    file_matches[file_path] = matches

name2asset = {asset.name: asset for asset in assets}
dependencies: list[Dependency] = []
term_uses: list[TermUse] = []
for asset, file_path in scans:
    for match in file_matches[file_path]:
        location = my_location.Location(
            file=file_path,
            loc_index=match.idx,
            loc_line=match.line,
            loc_column=match.column,
        )
        if match.target in name2asset:
            dependencies.append(
                Dependency(
                    location=location,
                    source_asset=asset,
                    target_asset=name2asset[match.target],
                    contexts=match.contexts,
                )
            )
        if match.target in cfg.blacklist:
            term_uses.append(TermUse(match.target, location, asset))

log.info('Found %d total dependency references.', len(dependencies))

items.title: Example 2.2 - Lint: blacklisted terms
items.text:
Report uses of blacklisted terms.

Blacklist (blacklist.json in the config directory) maps terms to the reason they shouldn't be used anymore: scripts and functions being phased out, assets that are about to be removed, etc. Uses are only reported, and are found the same way as asset references, so strings and comments don't count.

from clunkster import lint as my_lint

# see ex0.1 - Setup: Config
class Config: ...

# see ex1.2 - Lint: `tree.yyd` files
def lint_report(): ...

# see ex2.1 - Reference scanning
class TermUse: ...

RULE_BLACKLIST = my_lint.Rule(
    'B100', 'blacklisted term', my_lint.Severity.WARNING
)

# see ex2.1 - Reference scanning
term_uses: list[TermUse] = ...

violations = [
    my_lint.Violation(
        RULE_BLACKLIST,
        cfg.blacklist[use.term],
        location=use.location,
        asset=use.source_asset,
        group=use.term,
    )
    for use in term_uses
]
if violations:
    log.info('Found %d use(s) of blacklisted terms.', len(violations))
lint_report(cfg, violations)

items.title: Example 2.3 - Lint: unused assets
items.text:
Find and report assets that are never referenced by anything.

Removing unused assets is a quick way to clean up a project. We can do this with a simple set difference: Total Assets minus Used Assets. However, this will not catch isolated reference loops (e.g., A references B, B references A, but neither is used by the game). We'll handle these later.

Take the output of this with a grain of salt.

from clunkster import lint as my_lint
from clunkster.asset import Asset

# see ex0.1 - Setup: Config
class Config: ...

# see ex1.1 - Finding assets
class AssetExtAudio: ...
class AssetExtBgm: ...
class AssetExtSfx: ...
class AssetExtSfx3: ...

# see ex1.3 - Clusters
def asset_cluster_raw(): ...
def asset_cluster(): ...

# see ex2.1 - Reference scanning
class Dependency: ...

# see ex1.2 - Lint: `tree.yyd` files
def lint_report(): ...

RULE_UNUSED = my_lint.Rule('U100', 'unused asset', my_lint.Severity.WARNING)

# see ex1.3 - Clusters
assets: list[Asset] = ...

# see ex2.1 - Reference scanning
dependencies: list[Dependency] = ...

all_assets = {asset.name: asset for asset in assets}

# populate used set from dependencies
used_asset_names: set[str] = set()
for dep in progress(dependencies):
    # ignore self-references
    if dep.source_asset.name == dep.target_asset.name:
        continue
    used_asset_names.add(dep.target_asset.name)

orphan_names = set(all_assets.keys()) - used_asset_names
violations = [
    # group the report by cluster
    my_lint.Violation(
        RULE_UNUSED,
        asset=all_assets[name],
        group=asset_cluster(cfg, all_assets[name]),
    )
    for name in orphan_names
]

if violations:
    log.info('Found %d violations.', len(violations))
else:
    log.info('Somehow all clear...')
lint_report(cfg, violations)

items.title: Example 2.4 - Clusters: cross-cluster references
items.text:
Move assets referenced across cluster boundaries to Common.

Simple check of clusters on both ends of dependency edge will catch the majority of "stageA object referenced stageB asset" cases.

However, this check (and the following ones) have a few special rules:

  1. Most clusters are allowed to reference only themselves and Common cluster, but some may need to reference certain more localized "nonlocal" cluster. Such as when one collab maker creates multiple stages, and has many common scripts and util objects shared between them, but, technically, not between the rest of the collab. Such rules should be defined in LINT_RULES.

  2. We allow special context guard scripts in a form of:

if room_is_stageA() {
    ...
}
Those guards allow references to any foreign cluster inside them. Such guards must be defined in CONTEXT_RULES. Read more on those in the GML chapter.

  1. References to rooms are severed. Since the only way to meaningfully "instantiate" a room is to go there, for all intents and purposes whatever references a room doesn't really depend on it.

Instead of failing, an asset referenced from a cluster that isn't allowed to reference it is moved to Common: it stays in the base executable instead of being dehydrated, so the game can't run into its stub. A moved asset's own references are then checked as Common's, which may move more assets, until nothing changes. Moves are reported and their RAM is limited by a budget (see the report example below), since every moved asset is RAM the game always pays for. Fixing the reported references is still the way to get that RAM back.

import dataclasses

from clunkster import asset as my_asset
from clunkster.asset import Asset
from clunkster.text import location as my_location

# see ex0.1 - Setup: Config
class Config: ...

LINT_RULES: dict[str, set[str]] = {
    # common assets cannot borrow from Stage specific folders
    'Common': {'Common'},
    # example of a stage that shares assets with another
    # "StageB": {"StageB", "StageA", "Common"},
}


def allowed_clusters(cfg: Config, cluster: str) -> set[str]:
    """Get clusters that assets of the given cluster may reference.

    Defaults to the cluster itself and Common.
    """
    return set(cfg.lint_rules.get(cluster, {cluster, 'Common'}))

CONTEXT_RULES: dict[str, set[str]] = {
    'room_is_stageA': {'StageA'},
    'room_is_stageB': {'StageB'},
    'room_is_final': {'StageX', 'StageY', 'StageZ'},
    # rooms of lean clusters are granted by name, see guard_passes
    'room_is_stageC': {'StageC', 'rLeanRoomWithStageC'},
    # ...
}

# see ex1.1 - Finding assets
class AssetExtAudio: ...
class AssetExtBgm: ...
class AssetExtSfx: ...
class AssetExtSfx3: ...

# see ex1.3 - Clusters
def asset_cluster_raw(): ...
def asset_cluster(): ...

# see ex2.1 - Reference scanning
class Dependency: ...

@dataclasses.dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class Promotion:
    """Asset moved to Common because of a cluster violation."""

    asset: Asset
    # cluster the asset was in
    cluster: str
    # why it was moved
    reason: str
    location: my_location.Location | None = None
    # moved asset that caused this one to move, if any
    caused_by: str | None = None
    # extra lines for the report (e.g. traces)
    details: tuple[str, ...] = ()

# see ex2.1 - Reference scanning
dependencies: list[Dependency] = ...

def cluster_of(asset: Asset) -> str:
    if asset.name in promotions:
        return 'Common'
    return asset_cluster(cfg, asset)

def allowed_targets(dep: Dependency) -> set[str]:
    # permissions from lint rules
    allowed = allowed_clusters(cfg, cluster_of(dep.source_asset))
    # expanded based on script guards
    for ctx in dep.contexts:
        for primary in cfg.context_rules.get(ctx, ()):
            allowed.update(allowed_clusters(cfg, primary))
    return allowed

# references to rooms are severed
by_source: dict[str, list[Dependency]] = {}
for dep in dependencies:
    if not isinstance(dep.target_asset, my_asset.Room):
        by_source.setdefault(dep.source_asset.name, []).append(dep)

moved_before = len(promotions)
pending = list(by_source)
while pending:
    source_name = pending.pop()
    for dep in by_source[source_name]:
        target = dep.target_asset
        if target.name in promotions:
            continue
        target_cluster = cluster_of(target)
        if target_cluster in allowed_targets(dep):
            continue

        source = dep.source_asset
        source_moved = promotions.get(source.name)
        source_cluster = (
            cluster_of(source)
            if source_moved is None
            else f'{source_moved.cluster}, moved'
        )
        ctx = dep.contexts
        ctx_str = f' [Contexts: {", ".join(ctx)}]' if ctx else ''
        promotions[target.name] = Promotion(
            asset=target,
            cluster=target_cluster,
            reason=(
                f'referenced from {source.name} '
                f'[{source_cluster}]{ctx_str}'
            ),
            location=dep.location,
            caused_by=source.name if source.name in promotions else None,
        )
        # its own references now have to be allowed for Common
        if target.name in by_source:
            pending.append(target.name)

log.info('Moved %d asset(s) to Common', len(promotions) - moved_before)

Moved assets cost RAM, so it's still worth cleaning these up, which normally can take up to several days. I recommend giving Prerequisites a read - there are useful cleanup examples, as well as some explanations on how to write LINT_RULES and CONTEXT_RULES.

items.title: 3 - Dependency Graph
items.text: This section is about building a graph out of dependencies, and running checks based on more advanced usage tracing.

items.title: Example 3.1 - Generate dependency graphs
items.text:
Build dependency graph.

Reference scanner gave us a set of dependency edges, from which we can build a dependency graph. Graphs are done via rustworkx.

Our main application of this graph would be finding a set of used assets in each room, and feeding that info into linters.

There's two thing that makes this entire process a bit messy.
